title: This is my family
goal: Introduce your family, use the verb *mať*, and set up the rule that applies to every adjective in Slovak: its ending follows the gender of its noun.
bekal: name family members and their ages with *mať*
use *môj/moja/moje* and *ten/tá/to* with the right endings
form the nominative plural and see why male persons have an ending of their own

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Fotky v telefóne
dialogs.intro: Eva shows Budi photos of her family on her phone.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pekná fotka! Kto je ten pán?
lines.literal: nice-f photo! who is that-m gentleman?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: To je môj otec. Má päťdesiat rokov.
lines.literal: that is my-m father. he-has fifty years.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And the woman next to him?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: To je moja mama. Je učiteľka.
lines.id: That's my mother. She's a teacher.
lines.literal: that is my-f mother. she-is teacher-f.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do you have brothers and sisters?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Áno, mám brata a dve sestry. Tu sú.
lines.id: Yes, I have a brother and two sisters. Here they are.
lines.literal: yes, I-have brother and two sisters. here they-are.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What cute kids! Are they yours?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Nie, to sú deti mojej sestry. Nemám deti.
lines.id: No, those are my sister's kids. I don't have children.
lines.literal: no, those they-are children my-f-gen sister-gen. not-I-have children.

notes: **To je is used to point at anyone, anything.** Notice Eva says *to je môj otec* — not *ten je*. When you introduce or point, the form is always **to je** (singular) or **to sú** (plural), whatever the gender of what you're pointing at. *Toto* is a more emphatic form: "this, right here".

**Mať for age: literally "to have years".** *Má päťdesiat rokov* = "he has fifty years". Slovak counts age like French and Spanish, not like English. The question: *Koľko máš rokov?* — "How many years do you have?"

**Mám brata, not mám brat.** A verb's object changes the ending of its noun, and for **masculine nouns for living beings** the ending is *-a*. This is the accusative case, set out fully in the next unit. Notice also *peknú rodinu* and *veľkú rodinu* — the adjective and the noun change together.

**Nemám deti, not nemám dieťa.** Slovak uses the plural to say "I don't have children", because what's being denied is children in general. The word *dieťa* (child) has an irregular plural: *deti*, and that plural is **feminine**, even though the singular is neuter.

**Deti mojej sestry** = "my sister's children". Possession is shown by changing the ending of **the owner**, not with a word like "'s": literally "children of-my-sister". This is the genitive case, unit 9. For now just notice that the word that changes is the one **behind**.

grammars.title: Adjectives: one word, three endings
body: Every Slovak adjective adjusts its ending to the gender of the noun it describes. The good news: there are only three endings, very regular, and you've already met them in the four greetings of unit 1.
after: **Learn three letters: ý – á – é.** That's the core of it. If you know the noun's gender (unit 2), you know the adjective ending, with no exceptions.

**The last row is where male persons show up again.** The ordinary plural uses *-é*, but the plural for male persons uses *-í*, and the consonant before it often softens: *dobrý* → *dobrí*, *pekný* → *pekní*, *slovenský* → *slovenskí*. This is the part of A1 beginners most often ignore, and native speakers hear it very clearly.

**The rhythm rule applies here too.** If the syllable before the ending is already long, the ending is shortened: *krásny* (not *krásný*), *krásna* (not *krásná*), *krásne*. Compare *pekný, pekná, pekné*, whose first syllable is short. The rule is set out fully in unit 7.

grammars.title: My, your, and that
body: Possessives and demonstratives use the same ending pattern as adjectives, so you're not learning a new table — you're reusing one you already have.
after: **Three rows never change: *jeho*, *jej*, *ich*.** A small free gift. When you talk about what belongs to a third person, there's nothing to think about.
**The second form in the plural column is for male persons**, just like adjectives: *moji bratia* (my brothers), *naši učitelia* (our male teachers), but *moje sestry* and *naše knihy*.

**Ten/tá/to is not an article.** It means "that" and is used only when you're really pointing or contrasting: *Ten dom je pekný* = "**That** house is nice" (not the other one). To just say "the house is nice", *Dom je pekný* is enough. English speakers often sprinkle *ten* everywhere because they take it for *the*; don't.

blocks.text: Notice the **-ka** pattern that keeps coming up: *manžel → manželka*, *priateľ → priateľka*, *učiteľ → učiteľka*, *Slovák → Slovenka*. This ending makes a female counterpart for almost any noun for a person, and the result is always feminine. Once you know the male form, you practically get the female form for free.

blocks.title: Priateľ: friend or boyfriend?
items: Both, and the situation decides. *Môj priateľ* usually means "my boyfriend"; for just a male friend Slovaks more often say *kamarát* (f: *kamarátka*).
So when you introduce a classmate, say *toto je môj kamarát* — unless you really mean something else.

blocks.text: *Dcéra* is written with *d* and *c* in a row, but the *d* almost disappears in everyday speech: it sounds like *TSEH-rah*. This is one of the few words whose spelling isn't fully honest, and saying it letter by letter instantly marks you as a foreigner.
The basic plural — the one used as the subject of a sentence. Its ending is decided by the noun's gender, and once again male living beings stand apart.

**Only the first row needs attention.** The *-i* ending for male living beings softens the letter before it, and that softening sometimes changes the letter: *k → c* (*Slovák → Slováci*), *ch → s* (*Čech → Česi*), *h → z* (*sluha → sluhovia*). At A1 you only need to recognize it when you hear it, not produce it perfectly.

Some family words have plurals of their own that must be memorized: *brat → **bratia***, *dieťa → **deti***, *človek → **ľudia*** (person → people), *rodič → **rodičia***. All four are used constantly, so learning them now saves a lot of time.
Cover the Slovak column, read the English, and rebuild the Slovak sentence from memory. Only then uncover the column to check.

items: That's my father. He's a teacher.
Do you have brothers and sisters?

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right adjective ending.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Toto je moja rodina. — To je môj otec. Je učiteľ. — Máš súrodencov? — Mám dve sestry. — Má päťdesiat rokov. — Tie deti sú malé.
